title: Understanding Utility-Class Naming
subtopics: Utility names and their CSS equivalents
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of understanding utility-class naming.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on understanding utility-class naming and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: The reliability of understanding utility-class naming affects whether Tailwind detects candidate classes and generates the CSS you expect at build time.

content_blocks.title: Module 4 learning map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step module learning map: Understanding Utility-Class Naming → Understanding Variants → Handling Dynamic Class Names Correctly → Establishing a Reliable Utility-Class Workflow. Lesson pages add code examples and practice.
content_blocks.caption: Learning map for Module 4, from the opening concept to a practical checkpoint.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Utility names and their CSS equivalents; Property-oriented utility naming; Value scales; Utility combinations; Recognizing common naming patterns. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.expected_output: A theme variable defines a brand color; a configured build makes the matching utility available.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to understanding utility-class naming, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating understanding utility-class naming. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to understanding utility-class naming.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to understanding utility-class naming.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A theme variable defines a brand color; a configured build makes the matching utility available.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying understanding utility-class naming without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Understanding Utility-Class Naming is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
